"""Starting architecture: the main campaign's default policy (conv encoder, width 64, depth 2, ReLU,
no normalisation), rewritten as a candidate file. A 3x3 conv body, a 1x1 conv placement head
(one logit per brick type and anchor cell), and DONE and value heads on mean+max pooled features."""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

WIDTH = 64
DEPTH = 2


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        layers, c_in = [], spec.in_channels
        for _ in range(DEPTH):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(c_in, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
            c_in = WIDTH
        self.body = nn.Sequential(*layers)
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        place = self.place_head(f).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)

analyses.1: There are no trials yet. The baseline is bimodal: 3 of 4 seeds scored 0.068 and one scored 0.258. That suggests runs often get stuck in a local optimum rather than learning slowly. The default recipe makes only 32 PPO updates (256 envs × 16 steps = 4096 samples per update, 131k steps in total), which is very few policy-improvement steps, and the learning rate decays linearly. Fewer epochs buy more samples (2 epochs gives about 243k steps, 1 epoch about 426k steps), and smaller batches give more updates. The +1 exact-build bonus comes at the end of episodes up to 41 steps long, but gamma 0.95 looks only about 20 steps ahead, so a longer credit horizon may help. Round 1 tests three separate levers: more updates with fewer epochs, maximum samples with 1 epoch, and a longer horizon. Any gain below about 0.1 over the 0.116 baseline mean could be seed noise.
analyses.2: Every trial so far, and 3 of the 4 baseline seeds, ended at exactly 0.0684 dev success (35 of 512 designs). That means the trials converge to one fixed local optimum, probably a greedy fill of the missing cells that only works on designs where placement order or overhangs don't matter. One baseline seed escaped to 0.258. These results do not separate the recipes: changing epochs, sample count or update frequency (r1c1, r1c2) and lengthening the credit horizon (r1c3) all left the plateau unchanged, and in r1c3 training success fell further (0.041). The bottleneck looks like exploration: the policy collapses before it finds ordering behaviour. The levers left are entropy (to slow the collapse), a lower learning rate (gentler updates) and a combination of more samples with more entropy. A useful result is any seed above 0.0684. Another flat 0.068 pair is weak evidence against a lever.
analyses.3: Nearly every seed lands on the same 0.068 plateau, which looks like a greedy-fill policy that can't handle ordering or overhangs. Only three seeds out of 16 got past it: the baseline (0.258), r2c1 with entropy 0.03 (0.334) and r2c3 with 1 epoch and entropy 0.04 (0.121). The only lever with any sign of helping is the entropy bonus. Changing epochs or sample count alone, using a longer horizon, or lowering the learning rate did not help. Lower lr and the longer horizon both reduced training success. Because single seeds jump between 0.068 and about 0.3, 2-seed means are very noisy. What matters most is how often a seed escapes the plateau. This round keeps the strong-entropy default recipe and tests three things: more entropy, more gradient steps per update, and a higher learning rate. Each one is meant to raise the chance that a seed leaves the greedy mode before the policy commits.
analyses.4: The recipe changes split into two groups. The ones that did not touch entropy all stayed at or below the baseline: fewer epochs with more samples, a longer horizon (gamma 0.99), and lr 3e-4 (worst at 0.054). Raising the entropy coefficient is the first change that reliably got seeds past the 0.068 plateau (r2c1 0.20, r3c1 0.22, r3c2 0.22). Entropy 0.03 with lr 2e-3 (r3c3) got both seeds past it, at 0.334 and 0.416. That is well above the baseline's best seed (0.258), and its training success (0.20) is also the highest. So more exploration plus faster optimisation is what helps. lr 3e-4 hurt and lr 2e-3 helped, so the run is short of optimisation.
